claims.text: Equiatomic as-cast high-entropy alloys have inherent lattice distortions and baseline short-range order typical of conventional processing.
Controlled annealing and quenching can produce samples with enhanced short-range order relative to a conventionally processed baseline.
The dynamic balance of high strength and ductility in equiatomic high-entropy alloys is governed by reversible breakdown and recovery of short-range chemical order.
Dynamic loading temporarily disrupts regions of enhanced short-range order.
Disruption of short-range order facilitates dislocation nucleation.
Disruption of short-range order causes transient mechanical softening that promotes ductility.
Rapid reordering after disruption re-establishes barriers to dislocation motion.
Re-established barriers to dislocation motion restore alloy strength.
Relative to the baseline, an enhanced-SRO sample will show a more pronounced transient drop in flow stress at the onset of dynamic deformation.
The enhanced-SRO sample will show a rapid flow-stress increase after the initial transient softening.
In situ characterization of the enhanced-SRO sample will reveal more distinct cycles of dislocation nucleation and recovery of lattice order than in the baseline.
The proposed mechanism should operate at high strain rates, on the order of 10^3 s^-1, when short-range-order disruption and recovery occur on timescales competitive with deformation.
The proposed behavior may differ in non-equiatomic alloys or under quasi-static loading.
Twinning or phase transformation could complicate the predicted softening and hardening observations.
